Commit 6dbf7bb55598 (""fs: Don't invalidate page buffers in
block_write_full_page()"") uncovered a latent bug in ocfs2 conversion
from inline inode format to a normal inode format.
The code in ocfs2_convert_inline_data_to_extents() attempts to zero out
the whole cluster allocated for file data by grabbing
dirtying all pages covering this cluster.  However these pages are
beyond i_size
column2: thus writeback code generally ignores these dirty pages

column1: and no blocks were ever actually zeroed on the disk.
This oversight was fixed by commit 693c241a5f6a (""ocfs2: No need to zero
pages past i_size."") for standard ocfs2 write path
path was apparently forgotten; the commit log also has a reasoning why
the zeroing actually is not needed.
After commit 6dbf7bb55598
column2: things became worse as writeback code stopped

column1: invalidating buffers on pages beyond i_size and thus these pages end up
with clean PageDirty bit but with buffers attached to these pages being
still dirty.  So when a file is converted from inline format
writeback triggers
column2: and then the file is grown so that these pages

column1: become valid
column2: the invalid dirtiness state is preserved

column1: mark_buffer_dirty() does nothing on these pages (buffers are already
dirty) but page is never written back because it is clean.  So data
written to these pages is lost once pages are reclaimed.
Simple reproducer for the problem is:
xfs_io -f -c ""pwrite 0 2000"" -c ""pwrite 2000 2000"" -c ""fsync"" \
-c ""pwrite 4000 2000"" ocfs2_file
After unmounting and mounting the fs again
column2: you can observe that end of

column1: 'ocfs2_file' has lost its contents.
Fix the problem by not doing the pointless zeroing during conversion
from inline format similarly as in the standard write path.
